target: AG1’s claim that AI reliably improves daily life by reducing harm and expanding opportunity
objection: AI does not generally make society better because it causes significant economic harm by automating or deskilling work, weakening job security and the bargaining power of workers and small businesses, which can mean lower wages and more precarious employment rather than harm reduction.

target: AG1’s claim that AI makes work easier and therefore broadly expands opportunity
objection: AI undermines critical thinking by encouraging people to rely on algorithmic outputs instead of independently evaluating information, which can normalize uncritical acceptance of machine-generated claims and create downstream harms when those outputs are wrong or misleading.

target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits society overall without unacceptable discrimination
objection: AI can harm racial minorities by reproducing and amplifying biases already present in data and institutions, leading to predictable discriminatory outcomes in screening, recommendations, and risk assessment.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves society without major privacy downsides
objection: AI poses serious privacy risks because systems that collect large amounts of personal data can enable surveillance, re-identification, and misuse of sensitive information, so it does not reliably reduce harm overall.

target: AG1’s assumption that harmful effects are not inevitable and can be offset by responsible design and deployment
objection: Those harms are structurally persistent features of AI at scale, not mere deployment mistakes: fairness testing cannot guarantee non-discriminatory outcomes across contexts, privacy risks remain because AI depends on data aggregation and inference, and labor harms are driven by strong incentives to automate quickly.

target: AG1’s claim that AI reliably improves workplace safety by identifying risks and supporting safer procedures
objection: AI risk detection is not reliably accurate in safety-critical settings because models can miss rare hazards, produce false alarms that cause alarm fatigue, and trigger automation bias when workers over-trust machine recommendations, so accident risk is not reliably reduced overall.

target: AG1’s claim that AI reliably makes education and professional tasks easier in a way that expands opportunity
objection: AI does not reliably lower barriers to learning and work because access still depends on devices, connectivity, money, and digital literacy; the tools can also be unreliable or misleading in learning-critical contexts; and automation can reduce entry-level opportunities and job security.

target: AG1’s claim that AI reliably improves health outcomes and expands opportunity through medical support
objection: Medical AI is not reliably harm-reducing because it can be miscalibrated across different patient populations, clinicians may over-rely on wrong recommendations, and health applications also create privacy and data-use risks, so net benefit cannot be assumed.

target: AG1’s claim that AI reduces everyday friction, confusion, and information barriers in a reliable net-beneficial way
objection: AI often creates new everyday harms—wrong or unreliable outputs, hallucinated details, biased recommendations, fraud/scam risks, and privacy-invasive surveillance—so it can increase practical friction rather than reliably reduce it.

target: AG1’s claim that AI lowers costs and improves services in ways that broadly increase living standards
objection: AI can also hurt the economy by concentrating power in large incumbents: it often requires substantial data, compute, and integration resources that small businesses cannot match, which reduces competition and weakens workers’ bargaining power.

target: AG1’s claim that cloud-based AI tools reduce barriers enough to prevent harmful concentration
objection: Even if cloud services lower some upfront costs, AI still concentrates power through winner-take-most feedback loops and provider lock-in: larger firms get better through more usage data, while smaller firms depend on APIs and proprietary infrastructure controlled by incumbents.

target: AG1’s assumption that interoperability and modular tools prevent lock-in and concentration
objection: Lock-in is still systematic because switching providers changes model behavior and requires recalibration, retraining, and re-embedding workflows; many deployments also depend on provider-specific infrastructure, data pipelines, and compliance tooling that are costly to migrate.

target: AG1’s claim that larger user bases do not necessarily create a competitive advantage because training is centralized and data is siloed
objection: Even without continuous per-customer training, large deployments still generate proprietary feedback and evaluation signals that incumbents can use for periodic retraining, fine-tuning, and personalization, so scale can still produce a predictable performance advantage.

target: AG1’s claim that smaller firms can generate comparable feedback and use standard methods to compete on equal terms
objection: Larger incumbents get more diverse, higher-volume feedback and faster iteration, including rare edge cases, while smaller firms often rely on provider-controlled APIs and cannot retrain the base model or access the incumbent’s full update machinery, so the feedback advantage remains incumbent-favoring.

target: AG1’s claim that feedback-based improvements are broadly diffused so they do not create durable concentration
objection: Incumbents can keep feedback-derived gains persistent through phased rollouts, paid tiers, and proprietary deployment layers, meaning smaller firms may not get the same improvements promptly and provider-specific advantages can remain exclusive enough to weaken competition.
